world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is normally initial, but occurs on the second syllable of words having three or more syllables when the initial syllable is short, i.e. V or CV. A word is an isolatable syllable or group of syllables with one primary stress as defined above. Secondary stress is very light and varies freely.
new_statements.citation: Richert, Ernest & Marjorie Richert. 1972. Phonology of Guhu-Samane. Te Reo 15: 45-51. (Summer Institute of Linguistics)
new_statements.locator: §1.3 Stress, p. 47 (PDF page 3 of the 7-page scan; verified on the page image)
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word. It falls on the first syllable, except in words of three or more syllables whose first syllable is light (a single short vowel, V or CV), where it falls on the second syllable; a long (VV/CVV) initial syllable keeps initial stress, and disyllables are always initial-stressed. So: initial by default, with a weight-driven shift to the second syllable in longer words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Present but 'very light and varies freely' (no fixed position given).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The rule is worded 'normally initial', with the second-syllable case given as the only condition.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the authors define the word as 'an isolatable syllable or group of syllables with one primary stress'. Data from the Kipu dialect (the paper's §4, p. 49, names Kipu as the central, most widely used dialect; Richert lived at Kipu 1957-65 per Richert 1975 n. 2). §3 (p. 48) notes that in intonational pause groups non-final syllables have a neutral pitch 'affected by only a slight rise in pitch on the stressed syllables', so pitch is intonational, not lexical. Syllable types are V, VV, CV, CVV (p. 48), so 'short' = one vowel/mora, 'long' = VV.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Kipu dialect of Guhu-Samane (Richert & Richert 1972 §4, p. 49: 'The Kipu dialect of the Guhu-Samane language is the most central and widely used'; other dialects Bapi, Garaina, Sekare, Sinaba differ only slightly phonologically). Glottolog lists guhu1244 at language level with no separate Kipu glottocode found; ISO ghs. Warning: SIL archive 42421 'Guhu-Samane Organised Phonology Data' as archived by Wayback (2024-09-06) actually contains the Kela [Apoze] OPD (Oceanic) — its initial/antepenultimate stress line is not Guhu-Samane data.

sources.note: §1.3 Stress, p. 47: primary stress normally initial, but on the second syllable in words of three or more syllables whose initial syllable is short (V or CV); a word has one primary stress; secondary stress is very light and varies freely. §3 (p. 48) adds that non-final syllables carry a neutral pitch with only a slight rise on stressed syllables; intonation contours described for pause groups.

sources.citation: Smallhorn, Jacinta. 2011. The Binanderean languages of Papua New Guinea: reconstruction and subgrouping (Pacific Linguistics 625). Canberra: ANU. xvi+466 pp.
sources.note: Comparative work. §3.6 (pp. 79-80) surveys stress/tone in Binanderean (penultimate stress assumed for Proto Binandere non-verbs; phonemic stress with low functional load in Yekora, Baruga, Korafe; tone/pitch accent in Suena, Binandere). Chapter 5 (pp. 131 ff.) treats Guhu-Samane, gives its phoneme inventory from Richert & Richert 1972, but says nothing about Guhu-Samane stress.
